extracted.intended_audience: advanced undergraduates and graduate students in algebraic geometry
extracted.subtask_description: Guidance and exercises describing how to recognize and construct curves of low genus (primarily g=1..5), their canonical embeddings, moduli-dimension heuristics, automorphism properties, and classical descriptions (Weierstrass form, j-invariant, trigonal/hyperelliptic descriptions).

rubrics_metrics.name: Nonhyperelliptic genus 3 family dimension 6
rubrics_metrics.description: Give a heuristic (non-rigorous) argument that the nonhyperelliptic curves of genus 3 form a family of dimension 6.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Hint: Count the dimension of the family of regular quartic plane curves, and quotient by Aut P2 = PGL(3). Note context: hyperelliptic genus 3 curves form a family of dimension 5, but both fit into a single 6-dimensional family (hyperelliptic curves occur as limits).

rubrics_metrics.name: Hyperelliptic curves as limits of nonhyperelliptic curves
rubrics_metrics.description: Hyperelliptic curves are naturally limits of nonhyperelliptic curves: if a hyperelliptic curve is branched over 2g+2 points, choose an isomorphism of P1 with a conic in P2 and find a quartic meeting the conic at those points; the family f^2 + t^2 g of quartics is smooth for most t and at t=0 yields a double conic whose normalization is the hyperelliptic curve.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Uses Bertini’s theorem and generic smoothness; central fiber at t=0 is a double conic and normalization of total space recovers the hyperelliptic curve.

rubrics_metrics.name: Trigonal curve definition / trigonal criterion for genus 3
rubrics_metrics.description: A (projective) curve admitting a degree 3 cover of P1 is called trigonal. Every nonhyperelliptic genus 3 complex curve is trigonal.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Proof idea: take the quartic model in P2 and project to P1 from any point on the curve (choose coordinates so the point is [0,0,1]).

rubrics_metrics.name: Automorphisms of a smooth plane quartic vs automorphisms of P2 preserving it
rubrics_metrics.description: For a smooth plane quartic C' ⊂ P2, there is a bijection between automorphisms of C' and automorphisms of P2 preserving C' (as a set).
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Thus to control Aut(C') it suffices to study automorphisms of P2 fixing the quartic; most quartics have only the identity automorphism.

rubrics_metrics.name: Existence of genus 3 curves with no nontrivial automorphisms
rubrics_metrics.description: There exist genus 3 curves with no nontrivial automorphisms; most smooth quartics have this property; explicit examples can be given (e.g., y^3 z − 3 y z^3 = 3 x^4 − 4 x^3 z + z^4 over characteristic 0).
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Exhibit a specific smooth quartic and check that the only automorphism of P2 fixing it is the identity.

rubrics_metrics.name: Klein quartic and maximal automorphism count for genus 3
rubrics_metrics.description: The Klein quartic x^3 y + y^3 z + z^3 x = 0 in P2 has 168 automorphisms, and (using the fact that curves of genus >1 have finite automorphism groups) no genus 3 curve can have more automorphisms.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: The Klein quartic's automorphism group is the unique finite simple group of order 168; exercise: find all automorphisms.

rubrics_metrics.name: Genus 4 nonhyperelliptic canonical embedding as complete intersection
rubrics_metrics.description: A nonhyperelliptic genus 4 curve C has deg ωC = 6 and h^0(C, ωC) = 4, so the canonical map embeds C as a degree-6 curve in P3; such C are complete intersections of a quadric surface and a cubic surface, and conversely every regular complete intersection of quadric and cubic surfaces is a canonically embedded genus 4 nonhyperelliptic curve.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Argument uses Riemann–Roch/Serre duality to compute h0 values and linear algebra to produce a quadric containing C, then Bezout's theorem and Hilbert polynomial arguments to show the intersection equals C.

rubrics_metrics.name: Existence of a quadric containing genus 4 canonical curve
rubrics_metrics.description: For canonical genus 4 curve C ⊂ P3, h0(P3, OP3(2)) = 10 while h0(C, i^*OP3(2)) = 9, so the restriction map has nontrivial kernel and there is at least one quadric surface Q in P3 containing C. Q must be irreducible (not a plane).
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Quadrics of various ranks are considered; C cannot lie in a plane; arguments use rank classification and Bezout.

rubrics_metrics.name: OC(1) identifies with ωC for canonical genus 4
rubrics_metrics.description: If OC(1) has at least 4 sections (i.e., C does not lie in a hyperplane), then OC(1) ≅ ωC, so the given embedding is the canonical embedding.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Exercise 19.8.A: the only degree 2g−2 invertible sheaf with (at least) g sections is the dualizing sheaf (ωC).

rubrics_metrics.name: Heuristic dimension: nonhyperelliptic genus 4 family dimension 9
rubrics_metrics.description: Give a heuristic argument suggesting that the nonhyperelliptic curves of genus 4 form a family of dimension 9.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Count parameters of the complete intersection model and quotient by automorphisms; analogous to the genus-3 quartic counting.

rubrics_metrics.name: Genus 5 canonical curve degree and quadrics criterion
rubrics_metrics.description: A nonhyperelliptic genus 5 curve has canonical image of degree 8 in P4, and lies on a three-dimensional vector space of quadrics; a regular complete intersection of three quadrics is a canonically embedded genus 5 curve.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Compute h0 values via Riemann–Roch; exercise 19.8.C shows these dimension counts and the complete intersection criterion.

rubrics_metrics.name: Generic genus 5 canonical curves are cut out by 3 quadrics; trigonal exceptions
rubrics_metrics.description: Most canonical genus 5 curves are complete intersections of 3 quadrics; those that are not are precisely the trigonal curves—triples of points mapping to the same P1 point lie on a line in the canonical embedding, forcing quadrics vanishing on those points to vanish on the line.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: This describes the dense Zariski-open locus in the moduli space of genus 5 curves where the canonical embedding is cut out by 3 quadrics.

rubrics_metrics.name: Heuristic dimension: genus 5 family dimension 12
rubrics_metrics.description: Assuming the previous discussion, count complete intersections of three quadrics to give a heuristic argument suggesting that the curves of genus 5 form a family of dimension 12.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Exercise 19.8.D: parameter count minus projective automorphisms yields the heuristic.

rubrics_metrics.name: Canonical curve complete-intersection failure for g ≥ 6
rubrics_metrics.description: If g ≥ 6, then Pg−1 (the canonical curve of genus g) is not a complete intersection.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Exercise 19.8.E: use Bezout-type arguments to show canonical curves of higher genus fail to be complete intersections.

rubrics_metrics.name: Moduli dimension heuristic dim Mg = 3g − 3 (for g > 1)
rubrics_metrics.description: Heuristic/statement: the (stacky) dimension of the moduli space Mg of smooth projective geometrically irreducible genus g curves is 3g − 3 for g > 1.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Low-genus checks: dim M0 = 0, dim M1 = 1, computed heuristically dim M2 = 3, M3 = 6, M4 = 9, M5 = 12. Relation observed: dim Mg − dim Aut Cg = 3g − 3, since generic Aut Cg is 0-dimensional for g>1; genus 1 curves have 1-dimensional automorphism groups and genus 0 has 3-dimensional automorphism group.

rubrics_metrics.name: Genus 1: ωC degree and sections
rubrics_metrics.description: For a genus 1 curve C, deg ωC = 2g − 2 = 0 and h0(C, ωC) = g = 1; the only degree 0 invertible sheaf with a section is OC, thus ωC ≅ OC.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: This underpins subsequent descriptions of line bundles and embeddings for elliptic curves.

rubrics_metrics.name: Definition: elliptic curve includes marked point
rubrics_metrics.description: An elliptic curve is a genus 1 curve E together with a choice of a k-valued point p; the choice of this point is part of the definition (an unmarked genus 1 curve need not have k-valued points).
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Exercises and constructions assume the marked point when defining embeddings, group law, and correspondences with Pic0.

rubrics_metrics.name: Degree 1 line bundles correspond to degree 1 points; group law on E
rubrics_metrics.description: Each degree 1 (k-valued) point q determines a line bundle O(q); conversely every degree 1 line bundle is of the form O(q). The bijection between degree 1 line bundles and degree 1 points induces an abelian group structure on degree 1 points (Pic0 identification) with p as identity.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Proposition 19.9.3: identify closed points of E with degree 0 invertible sheaves and view Pic0(E) as the group variety to obtain the group law.

rubrics_metrics.name: Elliptic curves as double covers of P1 branched at 4 points
rubrics_metrics.description: If char k ≠ 2 and k is algebraically closed, OE(2p) has 2 sections so E admits a double cover of P1 branched at 4 points (one is p); conversely, given 4 points in P1 there exists a unique double cover branched at those 4 points.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Thus elliptic curves correspond to 4 distinct points in P1 (one marked), up to automorphisms of P1; after placing the marked point at infinity, one obtains 3 branch points in A1 up to affine maps.

rubrics_metrics.name: Cross-ratio λ parametrizes ordered 4-point configurations; S3-action and λ-equivalences
rubrics_metrics.description: For four ordered distinct points (P, Q1, Q2, Q3) on P1 one can send (P,Q1,Q2) to (∞,0,1) and the image of Q3 is λ (λ ≠ 0,1,∞); the six values related by the S3-action (λ, 1/λ, 1−λ, 1/(1−λ), (λ−1)/λ, λ/(λ−1)) give the same elliptic curve when considering unlabeled branch points.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Exercise 19.9.B and 19.9.C: cross-ratio classifies ordered configurations up to Aut P1; S4 action and Klein 4 subgroup remarks explain further symmetries.

rubrics_metrics.name: j-invariant as single invariant (function of λ)
rubrics_metrics.description: There exists a j-invariant j(λ) (rational function of λ) invariant under the S3-action so that j(λ) = j(λ') iff λ and λ' are related by the six expressions above; explicit formula given: j = 28 (λ^2 − λ + 1)^3 / (λ^2 (λ − 1)^2).
rubrics_metrics.guidance: j defines a degree-6 map from P1_λ to P1_j (for most λ the map is 6-to-1). The text discusses alternative symmetric constructions (sum of squares, second elementary symmetric function) and how the explicit rational expression arises; subtleties appear in characteristic 2 where constants like 28 matter.

rubrics_metrics.name: Weierstrass normal form for elliptic curves (char ≠ 2,3)
rubrics_metrics.description: If char k ≠ 2,3, after suitable coordinate changes an elliptic curve with a flex p can be written in Weierstrass normal form y^2 z = x^3 + a x z^2 + b z^3.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Coordinate choices: place p at [0,1,0] and the flex line at infinity z=0, then scale coefficients and perform linear changes to eliminate certain terms; the Weierstrass form makes explicit computations (e.g., j(a,b)) possible.

rubrics_metrics.name: j as function of Weierstrass coefficients (explicit formula)
rubrics_metrics.description: The j-invariant can be computed from Weierstrass coefficients a and b; the text gives an explicit rational expression j(a,b) = 2833 a^3 / (4 a^3 + 27 b^2) (as printed).
rubrics_metrics.guidance: This provides a concrete link between the cubic (Weierstrass) model parameters and the moduli invariant; caution: printed constants reflect characteristic considerations and normalization conventions.

rubrics_metrics.name: Geometric group law (chord-tangent) on an elliptic cubic
rubrics_metrics.description: If a line meets E at three points p1, p2, p3 then O(p1+p2+p3) ≅ O(3p) and in the group law p1 + p2 + p3 = 0; inverse and sum operations are given by chord-and-tangent constructions (third intersection point and reflection through origin).
rubrics_metrics.guidance: This gives a geometric, projective description of addition and inverse; associativity is justified via identification with Pic0(E) rather than direct algebraic verification.

rubrics_metrics.name: O(4p) embeds E in P3 as complete intersection of two quadrics
rubrics_metrics.description: The complete linear series for O(4p) embeds E in P3 as the complete intersection of two quadrics.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Exercise 19.9.E: show image lies in at least two linearly independent quadrics, neither reducible, and use Bezout/Hilbert polynomial arguments as in the genus-4 discussion.

rubrics_metrics.name: Degree-5 embedding structure and Pfaffian description
rubrics_metrics.description: The degree-5 embedding of E is not a complete intersection of hypersurfaces; it can be described as the intersection of the Grassmannian G(2,5) under its Plücker embedding with five hyperplanes, or equivalently by four 4×4 Pfaffians of a general 5×5 skew-symmetric matrix of linear forms.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: This indicates increasingly intricate projective models for higher-degree embeddings; the text sketches structure without full development.

rubrics_metrics.name: Elliptic curves are group varieties (algebraicity of operations)
rubrics_metrics.description: Addition and inverse on an elliptic curve are algebraic morphisms; elliptic curves are group varieties (abelian varieties).
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Proposition 19.10.2 and subsequent discussion: show inverse map arises from a morphism; algebraicity of addition is shown by geometric constructions combined with general tricks rather than writing formulas explicitly.

rubrics_metrics.name: Third-intersection morphism t on regular cubic curves (Proposition 19.10.3)
rubrics_metrics.description: For a geometrically integral cubic curve C with regular locus C_reg, there is a unique morphism t : C_reg × C_reg → C_reg such that: (a) for distinct regular k-points p,q, t(p,q) is the third residual intersection point of the line pq with C; (b) property remains true after any field extension; for p=q, t(p,p) is the third intersection of the tangent line at p with C.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Construction uses explicit affine-local algebra (write line x2 = m x1 + b, substitute into cubic, use Viète to get third root), Zariski-open conditions to define morphism, and descent to arbitrary fields; this morphism underlies algebraic description of chord-tangent addition.
